column3: God extends the misguided until the promised outcome appears, giving a contrary divine use of extension before judgment.
Pharaoh's attempt to build toward the means of heaven closely parallels a false vertical device aimed at what lies beyond his control.
It contrasts an uncontrolled extending gaze with a redirected, protective attention, offering a secondary affective counterpoint.
God alone holds recompense in this world and the next, supporting the focus's insistence that aid across both is not humanly controlled.
The nearby warning that allegiance to the rebellious satan leads to ruin supplies the passage's false-attachment background.
It supplies only the word and stance of hostile rage, without the focus's failed device or divine aid.
A mistaken assumption about God's power is answered by confession and rescue, furnishing a sharp contrary response to the focus's assumption.
The immediately preceding dispute without knowledge and following of rebellious satan identifies the hostile posture surrounding the focus.
It directly states that their plotting will avail nothing and that they will not be helped, clarifying the failure asserted in the focus.
The completed tower scene joins heavenly means, a false assumption, and Pharaoh's perishing plot in a close parallel to the focus's device.
The promise of forgiveness and generous provision does not clarify the focus's challenge concerning aid, severing, or rage.
It shows God cutting down or humiliating disbelievers, distinguishing effective divine cutting from the focus figure's futile attempt.
Its loss of works in this world and the next and absence of helpers form a broad negative counterpart to God's aid.
Satan's manufacture of fear and the command to redirect fear to God illuminate a hostile inward pressure without granting it control.
God's total command and the certainty of His promise counter any attempt to force or obstruct the divine outcome.
The destruction of the idol uses removal and cutting imagery but concerns a distinct scene of idolatry.
Holding fast to God, the patron and helper, supplies the passage's explicit positive alternative to a self-defeating attachment.
God's sufficiency as guide and helper against hostile enemies gives a general assurance underlying the focus.
Punishment in this world and the next with no helpers supplies a broad contrary fate to divinely supported people.
This nearby portrait of one who misleads from God's way and receives disgrace and punishment reinforces the surah's hostile resistance theme.
Following a means is only a lexical and procedural contrast to the focus's destructive use of a means.
The command to inspect human creation adds no meaningful link to divine aid or the failed plot.
The pilgrimage summons does not clarify the focus's device, rage, or claim about aid.
This repeated following of a means remains a distant, already redundant contrast to the focus's upward means.
The description of clouds and hail does not add to the focus's relation of plot and divine aid.
God's ongoing provision offers only a broad contrast to the focus's attempt to manage a source of support.
The earth being spread out has no material connection beyond a shared extension root.
The command to look at food does not clarify the focus's final command to inspect a plot.
The nearby conditional worshiper who turns away under trial strongly explains the unstable attachment and worldly-otherworldly stakes around the focus.
God's removal of believers' heart-rage provides a direct positive counterpart to the focus's question whether plotting can remove rage.
Ungrateful resentment despite divine enrichment, followed by punishment and no helper, adds a related portrait of hostile grievance.
It explicitly promises that God will help one wronged after retaliation, directly affirming the aid doubted in the focus.
Their deliberate plotting directly names the hostile action that the focus declares ineffective.
The world's apparent mastery collapsing under God's command only broadly parallels the focus's false assumption of control.
Divine extension of material support is a distant contrast to extending a means for a futile scheme.
Extended columns provide only a structural echo of the focus's extension, without its aid or rage relation.
A false expectation before resurrection is only a general analogue to mistaken supposition.
The distinction between outward material and the inward reality God receives supports the focus's exposure of an outward act that cannot alter the real issue.
God does not guide the plot of betrayers, giving a direct general rule for the focus's failed plotting.
The challenge to produce any plot is a concise parallel challenge, though it lacks the focus's aid and severing image.
The statement of divine bounty and success does not materially illuminate the focus.
The absence of mutual aid is a brief, broad contrast to the focus's question of divine aid.
Pharaoh's gathering of a plot adds another hostile scheme but is less informative after the fuller tower account.
The punishment image does not clarify the focus's mechanism of failed resentment.
A third instance of following a means is a redundant procedural contrast to the focus's severing of one.
Good deeds removing evil offers a distant ethical alternative to trying to remove inward anger by plotting.
Those who obstruct their kin from danger offer a secondary image of internal obstruction and withdrawn support.
The categorical assurance that God's servants are helped states the positive certainty opposed to the focus's doubt.
The instruction to inspect food is unrelated to the focus's test of a scheme.
The warning of the Hour's earthquake does not explain the focus's claim about aid or rage.
It explicitly calls Satan's plot weak, directly supporting the focus's exposure of hostile scheming as ineffective.
The question about a table from heaven only loosely echoes seeking something from above and lacks the focus's issue.
Blocking God's way and incurring punishment extends the surah's portrait of hostile opposition, though not the focus's particular device.
God returns disbelievers with their rage while they gain no good and suffices the believers, closely matching failed rage-driven opposition.
Believers' costly action that enrages disbelievers is counted as righteous, offering a distinct account of rage without conceding it power.
The spreading and balancing of the earth does not clarify the focus's self-defeating extension.
Means are granted by God as usable capacities, contrasting the focus's imagined private control over a means.
God's promise to help those who help Him is the surah's direct affirmation of the aid whose denial drives the focus challenge.
The terror of the divine punishment does not add to the focus's device or inward rage.
Lot's appeal for divine help against corrupters provides a concrete prayerful alternative to hostile self-reliance.
The question whether false gods can help exposes the inadequacy of rival sources of aid.
Deferring opponents to their destructive day gives only a general judgment backdrop.
The cut of night in Lot's departure is a different temporal usage with no explanatory role here.
God's strength and the testing of who helps Him and His messengers adds a distinct reciprocal account of divine support.
God's counterplot immediately answers human plotting, giving the clearest broader pattern for the focus's failed scheme.
God extends punishment in answer to arrogant speech, a distinct reversal of the focus figure's attempted extension.
Fearful reluctance toward fighting and preference for the world offer only a broad contrast to reliance on God's command.
The description of untroubling drink does not bear on the focus's plot or aid.
On the decisive day no patron can avail another and none are helped, delimiting all non-divine support.
God alone provides from heaven and earth, grounding the focus's contrast between divine provision and human control.
God's conclusive proof and power to guide give a broad sovereignty backdrop but no specific plot relation.
Believers' flourishing enrages disbelievers, furnishing a distinct outcome for the rage named in the focus.
The passage directly rebukes an unsound assumption about God and asserts that all command belongs to Him, closely clarifying the focus's supposition.
At punishment, the means between followers and leaders are cut; this supplies a consequential contrast to the focus's proposed severing of a means.
Demanding to see God openly and the resulting punishment does not explain the focus's challenged plot.
God's help against enemies and healing of believers' hearts revisits the direct divine removal of rage from a different angle.
The women's cutting of hands and a known plot are a distant lexical overlap without the focus's support relation.
The prophet's challenge to adversaries to plot against him is a general hostile-plot parallel only.
The invitation to purification does not clarify the focus's issue.
God's sole dominion and the absence of any protector or helper besides Him give a direct theological boundary for the focus.
Divine protection in Lot's escape is only indirectly related; the cutting is a portion of night, not the focus's device.
Condemning the cutting of what God ordered joined distinguishes destructive severance from rightful attachment, though at a broad level.
The demand for a book from heaven is a remote sky-image with no aid or failed-plot connection.
Abraham's declared plan against idols is a different kind of plot and adds only contrast evidence.
The Israelites' refusal to enter the land does not clarify the focus's challenge.
Severing kinship ties and corruption are a distant moral analogue to severing a means.
The Fire's rage is distinct from the inward rage the focus says plotting cannot remove.
Those cursed by God find no helper, reinforcing the limit on aid outside divine favor.
The contrast between worldly and otherworldly harvest gives only a broad horizon shared with the focus.
God turns away a hostile plot in response to prayer, providing a concrete pattern of divine protection against scheming.
Satanic teaching and harm only by God's permission offer a broad constraint on hostile powers.
The cutting of intestines in punishment is unrelated to the focus's figurative severing of a means.
The legal account of nursing and support does not clarify the focus's plot or divine aid.
Authorized cutting of trees differs from the focus's futile self-directed cutting, giving only a remote contrast.
Obedience, forgiveness, and success do not add a specific relation to the focus.
The call to help idols is a contrary, false appeal for support but lacks the focus's mechanism.
The domestic privacy rule has no meaningful relation to the focus.
The Fire's rage is a distinct scene and only a lexical echo of the focus's inward anger.
The clothing and modesty instruction does not illuminate the focus.
The hypocrites' promise to help allies is exposed as false, contrasting unreliable human pledges with the divine aid at issue.
It explicitly states that none can overcome those helped by God and none can help those He forsakes, directly resolving the focus's premise.
The believers' declaration that God is sufficient supplies the trusting alternative to trying to manage the outcome through a private scheme.
It assures believers that hostile plotting will not harm them with patience and God-consciousness, giving a direct boundary on the focus figure's plot.
It confines victory and reassurance to God, making divine help rather than human contrivance the decisive source.
Their planning is met by God's planning, directly extending the focus's claim that hostile design cannot control the result.
God's help in a moment of apparent isolation gives a concrete narrative counterexample to the assumption that His support will fail.
God is dominant over His affair, sharply limiting the focus figure's imagined ability to interrupt what God brings about.
The opponents' plot is answered by an unperceived divine counterplan, preserving the same confrontation between human scheme and divine governance.
God's stated commitment to help believers directly affirms the aid whose absence is supposed in the focus.
The evil plot ultimately encloses only its own makers, closely expressing the self-defeating reversal suggested by the focus's device.
The reciprocal promise that aiding God's cause brings God's aid supplies the positive form of the support relation at issue.
God's decree that He and His messengers will prevail gives a categorical answer to any effort to defeat divine support.
Reliance on God is declared sufficient, directly contrasting dependence on Him with the focus figure's futile constructed means.
Calling on what can neither harm nor benefit portrays the false attachment that immediately precedes and clarifies the focus's challenge.
The condemnation of a harmful, bad patron and companion makes explicit the passage's contrast between false patronage and God's support.
God's defense of the believers is an immediate-surah assurance of protective action against the hostile posture exposed in the focus.
